findings.lesson_text: Quickly says Falstaff's heart was 'fracted and corroborate' (broken).
findings.issue: The lesson attributes 'fracted and corroborate' to Mistress Quickly (in the context of the Act 2, Scene 3 death report). The line is spoken by Pistol, not Mistress Quickly, and it appears in Act 2, Scene 1 — not Scene 3. In Scene 1, Nym says 'The King hath run bad humours on the knight', and Pistol responds: 'Nym, thou hast spoke the right; His heart is fracted and corroborate.' Mistress Quickly's account of Falstaff's death in Act 2, Scene 3 contains 'babbled of green fields' and physical detail about his death, but she never says 'fracted and corroborate'.
findings.canonical_truth: Act 2, Scene 1: Pistol says 'His heart is fracted and corroborate' — referring to Falstaff's broken spirit after Henry's rejection. This is spoken before Falstaff dies. Act 2, Scene 3: Mistress Quickly reports Falstaff's death, describing 'his nose was as sharp as a pen, and a' babbled of green fields.' The two quotations are in different scenes and spoken by different characters.

findings.lesson_text: Canterbury and the Bishop of Ely have a private conversation beforehand (Act 1, Scene 1) revealing that they support the war partly to protect Church lands from a parliamentary bill. [...] Canterbury delivers a famously tedious speech about the Salic Law to justify Henry's claim to the French throne.
findings.issue: The lesson collapses two separate scenes. The private conversation between Canterbury and Ely about protecting Church lands is correctly placed in Act 1, Scene 1. However, the lesson then places the Salic Law speech in the same section without clearly distinguishing that it occurs in Act 1, Scene 2 (before the King and court), not Scene 1. A student might misread the lesson as placing the Salic Law speech in Act 1, Scene 1.
findings.canonical_truth: Act 1, Scene 1: Canterbury and Ely speak privately about a parliamentary bill threatening Church revenues and agree to encourage Henry's war to deflect it. Act 1, Scene 2: Canterbury delivers the Salic Law speech before Henry and his court. These are two separate scenes with different audiences and purposes. The lesson's structure conflates them.

findings.lesson_text: Shakespeare introduces four captains from the four nations of Britain: Fluellen (Welsh), Gower (English), Macmorris (Irish) and Jamy (Scottish).
findings.issue: The lesson does not specify where the four captains appear together — implying it is during the Harfleur section broadly. In fact all four captains appear together in Act 3, Scene 2 (immediately after Henry's 'Once more unto the breach' speech in Act 3, Scene 1). The lesson bundles this into the Harfleur section without giving the scene number, which is accurate at the act level but imprecise.
findings.canonical_truth: The four captains (Fluellen, Gower, Macmorris, Jamy) all appear together in Act 3, Scene 2. Macmorris delivers 'What ish my nation?' in this scene. Fluellen continues to appear in Acts 3, 4 and 5, but the multi-captain scene establishing the four-nation framework is Act 3, Scene 2.

findings.lesson_text: Henry's order to kill the French prisoners [...] given in response to a French attack on the English baggage train
findings.issue: The lesson presents the baggage-train attack as the established reason for Henry's prisoner order ('Then every soldier kill his prisoners!'). Chronologically in the play, the prisoner order appears in Act 4, Scene 6 (before Fluellen and Gower discover the baggage attack in Act 4, Scene 7). Most scholarly readings and the historical record indicate Henry gives the order because he feared the French prisoners would re-arm. Shakespeare actually reverses or conflates the chronology — the lesson presents a causal link the text does not firmly establish. Fluellen in Act 4, Scene 7 retrospectively links them ('the King, most worthily, hath caused every soldier to cut his prisoner's throat'), but the dramatic order has the prisoner command first, the baggage discovery second.
findings.canonical_truth: In the play, Act 4 Scene 6: Henry gives the order to kill prisoners. Act 4 Scene 7: Fluellen and Gower discover the French have attacked the baggage train and killed the boys. Fluellen then connects the two events retrospectively, but the prisoner order comes first dramatically. Historically, chronicles disagree on the cause. The lesson's phrasing 'given in response to a French attack' implies a clear causation that is more ambiguous in the text itself.

findings.lesson_text: His comparison of Henry to 'Alexander the Pig' (meaning 'Big') is funny but also flattering.
findings.issue: The lesson notes the comparison is 'funny but also flattering' but omits the darker subtext Shakespeare builds into the scene. Fluellen's 'Alexander the Pig' speech (Act 4, Scene 7) proceeds to note that Alexander killed his best friend Cleitus — drawing a pointed parallel to Henry's rejection of Falstaff. The lesson presents the comparison as purely comic and flattering, missing the dramatic irony that makes the scene significant for character analysis.
findings.canonical_truth: In Act 4, Scene 7, Fluellen compares Henry to 'Alexander the Pig' (Alexander the Great). The speech continues: Fluellen acknowledges that Alexander killed his best friend in a rage ('turn away the fat knight with the great belly doublet... I speak but in the figures and comparisons of it: as Alexander killed his friend Cleitus, being in his ales and his angers, look you, so also Harry Monmouth, being in his right wits and his good judgements, turned away the fat knight with the great belly doublet'). The comparison is both comic and an implied criticism of Henry's cold rejection of Falstaff.

findings.lesson_text: Henry V 'lived but a short time' and his son, Henry VI, 'lost France and made his England bleed, / Which oft our stage hath shown.'
findings.issue: The lesson paraphrases the Epilogue using quotation marks that mix paraphrase and quotation. The actual Epilogue does not say 'lived but a short time' — that phrase is a paraphrase. The Epilogue's exact lines are: 'Henry the Sixth, in infant bands crowned King / Of France and England, did this king succeed, / Whose state so many had the managing / That they lost France and made his England bleed.' The lesson presents the paraphrase 'lived but a short time' inside the quotation block alongside accurate quotation, which could mislead students into memorising an invented phrase.
findings.canonical_truth: Epilogue exact text (Chorus, sonnet form): 'Thus far with rough and all-unable pen / Our bending author hath pursued the story, / In little room confining mighty men, / Mangling by starts the full course of their glory. / Small time, but in that small most greatly lived / This star of England: Fortune made his sword; / By which the world's best garden he achieved, / And of it left his son imperial lord. / Henry the Sixth, in infant bands crowned King / Of France and England, did this king succeed, / Whose state so many had the managing / That they lost France and made his England bleed; / Which oft our stage hath shown; and, for their sake, / In your fair minds let this acceptance take.' The phrase is 'Small time, but in that small most greatly lived' — not 'lived but a short time'.

findings.lesson_title: Context: Tudor Propaganda & the History Play
findings.lesson_text: The Chorus explicitly references Essex in Act 5 ("the General of our gracious Empress").
findings.issue: The Essex reference appears in the Act 5 Chorus (i.e. the Chorus that precedes Act 5, sometimes cited as 5.0 or 5.Chor.), not within Act 5 itself. This is a minor labelling ambiguity — the Chorus is technically the prologue to Act 5, not part of the act's scenes — but the lesson's phrasing 'in Act 5' could lead students to look in the Act 5 scenes rather than the Chorus.
findings.canonical_truth: The Essex reference ('Were now the general of our gracious empress') appears in the Chorus that introduces Act 5 (Act 5, Prologue/Chorus, lines 30-34), not within the scenes of Act 5. In performance and scholarship it is typically cited as 'Act 5, Prologue' or '5.0.30-31'. The phrase is 'the general of our gracious Empress' (not 'the General').
